chain.g: to wave, fluctuate, waver in mind, wonder
to move to and from, wander

ety.text: From Middle English waven, from Old English wafian (“to wave, fluctuate, waver in mind, wonder”), from Proto-West Germanic *wabōn, from Proto-Germanic *wabōną, *wabjaną (“to wander, sway”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move to and from, wander”). Cognate with Middle High German waben (“to wave”), German wabern (“to waft”), Icelandic váfa (“to fluctuate, waver, doubt”). See also waver.

chain.g: a wave, billow, motion, water, flood, sea

ety.text: From Middle English *wave, partially from waven (“to fluctuate, wave”) (see above) and partially from Middle English wawe, waghe (“wave”), from Old English wǣg (“a wave, billow, motion, water, flood, sea”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“motion, storm, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to drag, carry”).

senses.d: To move back and forth repeatedly and somewhat loosely.
ex: The flag waved in the gentle breeze.

senses.d: To move one's hand back and forth (generally above the shoulders) in greeting or departure.
To call attention to, or give a direction or command to, by a waving motion, as of the hand; to signify by waving; to beckon; to signal; to indicate.
ex: I waved goodbye from across the room.
Look, with what courteous action / It waves you to a more removed ground.

senses.d: To have an undulating or wavy form.
To raise into inequalities of surface; to give an undulating form or surface to.
ex: horns whelked and waved like the enridged sea

senses.d: To style (the hair) so as to produce a wavy texture.
To swing and miss at a pitch.
ex: Jones waves at strike one.

senses.d: To cause to move back and forth repeatedly.
ex: The starter waved the flag to begin the race.
His father has waved bills in front of face and said to him — see what you've cost me.

senses.d: To signal (someone or something) with a waving movement.
To fluctuate; to waver; to be in an unsettled state.
ex: He waved indifferently 'twixt doing them neither good nor harm.

senses.d: A moving disturbance in the level of a body of liquid; an undulation.
ex: The wave traveled from the center of the lake before breaking on the shore.
O God! can I not save / One from the pitiless wave? / Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?

senses.d: The ocean.
ex: Whoever rules the waves rules the world...

senses.d: A moving disturbance in the energy level of a field.
ex: Gravity waves, while predicted by theory for decades, have been notoriously difficult to detect.

senses.d: A shape that alternatingly curves in opposite directions.
ex: Her hair had a nice wave to it.
sine wave

senses.d: Any of a number of species of moths in the geometrid subfamily Sterrhinae, which have wavy markings on the wings.
A loose back-and-forth movement, as of the hands.
ex: He dismissed her with a wave of the hand.

senses.d: A sudden, but temporary, uptick in something.
ex: A wave of shoppers stampeded through the door when the store opened for its Christmas discount special.
A wave of retirees began moving to the coastal area.

senses.d: Any of a series of orders to be fulfilled in one short interval of time, planned as part of wave picking.
A movement or trend in popular culture.
ex: New Wave
Korean Wave

senses.d: One of the successive swarms of enemies sent to attack the player in certain games.
ex: As the player eliminates each wave of 55 aliens, the next wave begins lower than the one previous.

senses.d: To generate a wave.
ex: If the electron had wavelike properties, then what was disturbing the medium in which the wave existed? What was waving?
